question: Which writer owns creation of session-state.json, given that ai_router/session_state.py and the extension's utils/sessionState.ts both create it and the extension's copy is reached from a READ (readStatus)?
decision: The router's sanctioned writers own creation. The extension's read path stops writing: readStatus derives the same shape in memory (inferStateInMemory) and readSessionSets uses that derivation when the file is absent. ensureSessionStateFile is removed from the extension; synthesizeNotStartedState survives as an explicit-action writer only, and cancel/restore keep their own sanctioned writer. The rule: the extension writes session-state.json only on an explicit operator action, never on a read. Reversible cheaply — the removed write is one function and its call site, and the in-memory builder is the same code path the writer used.

options.option: Keep both writers and mirror the title logic, enforced by a parity test
options.consequence: The race survives: whichever writer reaches disk first still decides the ledger, and the next field added to the payload re-opens the same defect. Parity would prove agreement about titles, not about who writes.

options.option: Router owns creation; the extension's read derives in memory (chosen)
options.consequence: The race cannot happen — a scan produces no file at all. Removes a writer and an untracked-file side effect Set 099 S2 had already worked around with rawSessionSetStatus. Costs an in-memory branch in readSessionSets so spec-only sets keep their planned rows, and changes three tests that pinned the write side effect.

options.option: Extension owns creation; strip the Python lazy-synth
options.consequence: Inverts the constitution's state-mutation discipline (start_session / close_session are the sanctioned writers) and would leave consumer repos without a state file whenever the Explorer is not open.

question: A generic `Session N` title is sticky because title resolution puts the stored ledger first. 130 rows across the repo carry one, and most belong to CLOSED sets that will never get another boundary write. Where does the heal go, given spec decision 4 says this set does not move title resolution onto the read path?
decision: Heal in BOTH places through one shared pure rule (progress.heal_title, mirrored in progress.ts). The writer heals at every boundary write so the fix persists; the reader heals the display so closed sets — which get no further write — stop lying, with no migration script rewriting closed history. The reader's spec read is CONDITIONAL on needs_title_heal, so a healthy set costs no additional disk read, which is the measured constraint decision 4 was protecting. Reversible: the read-path heal is one guarded block per language.

options.option: Write-path heal only, honouring decision 4 literally
options.consequence: Fails this session's own Ends-with ('existing sets heal themselves'): ~130 rows in closed sets never get another boundary write and stay generic forever.

options.option: Write-path heal plus a conditional read-path heal (chosen)
options.consequence: Every set displays its real titles immediately, including closed ones. Costs one spec read per DRIFTED set per scan and none for healthy sets; the existing readSessionSets perf gate (p95 < 5000ms) is the falsifier.

options.option: A one-shot migration script that rewrites every drifted state file
options.consequence: Rewrites closed sets' records — the thing this repo treats as history — and the spec explicitly asks for healing WITHOUT a migration script. Also leaves the write-path bug in place for the next set.

question: Does the session-scoped reveal need a NEW command and its own file-opening path, or should it go through the existing `dabblerSessionSets.openSpec`?
decision: One command, two callers. `dabblerSessionSets.openSpec` learned to read a session number off its argument (`kind: "session"`) and to open `spec.md` positioned at that session's `### Session N of M:` block; a set node through the same command still opens at the top, byte-identical to before. The tree-level command `dabblerWorkExplorer.activateSession` exists only to narrow the untrusted node and dispatch — the exact shape `activateSet` already has. The heading scan is BORROWED from `sessionStepModel.scanSessionHeads` (mirror of `spec_admission._SESSION_HEAD_RE`) rather than re-derived, so one regex decides where session 3 begins.

options.option: A parallel `openSessionSpec` command with its own existence check, message wording and file resolution
options.consequence: A second place to answer 'which file is the spec' and a second 'Spec does not exist yet' message to keep in sync; the two drift the first time either changes.

options.option: Teach the existing openSpec to take an optional section (chosen)
options.consequence: One file-resolution path, one message, one heading regex shared with the step parser. Costs a narrowing helper that FAILS CLOSED — anything that is not a session node carrying a positive integer opens at the top.

options.option: Spawn the Python extractor (`verify_session.extract_spec_excerpt`) for the section
options.consequence: Puts a process spawn on a click and makes a display feature fail whenever the interpreter is unresolvable — the coupling Set 114 S3 rejected for the step rows.

question: Step 4 asks whether the plain reveal reads as too unfocused in use — and if it does, a read-only virtual document on a custom scheme is the sanctioned next step. Ship the custom scheme now, or ship the plain reveal and let the set's own UAT answer it?
decision: Ship the plain reveal, and record that the question is ANSWERED BY THE OPERATOR at this set's UAT walk, not by the orchestrator's guess. The reveal is deliberate rather than incidental — `showTextDocument` + `revealRange(AtTop)` puts the session's own heading on the first viewport row (proven in a real host, `session-plan-reveal.spec.ts`), and the selection is left EMPTY so no 40-line highlight is painted over a file the operator is about to read. That is the strongest form of 'the plain reveal' available, so if it still reads as unfocused, the finding is about the FORMAT and not about the implementation. No custom scheme is added on this evidence: the spec's non-goals refuse one 'unless Session 2 measures the plain reveal as insufficient', and nothing measured here is insufficient — the operator lands in the real file, at the real section, with the surrounding context and the configuration block a scroll away, which is exactly what decisions 1-3 bought.

options.option: Ship the plain reveal; the set's UAT walk decides whether it is focused enough (chosen)
options.consequence: Zero new surface, and the question stays open on evidence rather than being closed by a reflex. If the walk says it is unfocused, the custom scheme is a recorded follow-up with a named reason — which is what the spec asks for.

options.option: Add a read-only virtual document on a custom scheme now
options.consequence: A second rendering of the truth on screen, a new scheme to register and keep alive, and the operator loses the surrounding spec context the set explicitly chose to keep. Taken pre-emptively it would be the 'default, not a decision' the spec warns against.

options.option: Select the whole session block instead of placing an empty cursor
options.consequence: More visibly 'focused' for one second, then a large highlight over unread text that the first keystroke would replace. Rejected as a worse default, not deferred.

question: Step 3 says gate the session run prompt on status the way `planLeftClickActivation` does. Taken literally that puts "Copy Run Prompt" on EVERY non-terminal session row. But the framework's only documented run trigger is set-scoped â€” `Start the next session of `<slug>`.` (workflow doc, Trigger Phrases) â€” so on session 4 while session 3 is next, that prompt starts a DIFFERENT session than the row it was copied from. Offer the prompt on every non-terminal session, invent a session-scoped trigger phrase, or gate it to the session the phrase would actually run?
decision: Gate it to the session the phrase actually runs, and copy the documented phrase verbatim. The action's `when` is the conjunction of two existing rules and one new one: the set-level gate is `planLeftClickActivation(set.name, set.state).clipboardWrite !== null` â€” reused, not re-implemented, so the set row and the session row cannot drift on what a runnable set is â€” and the session-level rule is `nextRunnableSessionNumber(sessions)`: walk the ledger in ascending number order, skip `complete` and `cancelled`, and the first survivor is the candidate; it is runnable only if its status is `in-progress` or `not-started`. An unrecognised status therefore yields NO offer anywhere in the set, which is the fail-closed posture step 3 names. The copied text is `buildStartNextSessionPrompt(set)` â€” the same builder the set row's L5 shortcut uses. No new trigger-phrase vocabulary is minted.

options.option: Gate to the next runnable session; copy the documented set-scoped phrase (chosen)
options.consequence: The prompt on a row always starts THAT row's session, because the only row that carries it is the one the phrase resolves to. Costs discoverability: sessions 4..N show no run prompt. That is honest â€” they are not runnable yet, and the workflow is strictly sequential (`start_session` infers max(closed)+1).

options.option: Offer on every non-terminal session, copying the same set-scoped phrase
options.consequence: A lie by placement: pasting the prompt copied from session 4 starts session 3. This is precisely the class of defect the repo's documentation-authority principle exists to prevent, and the operator would only discover it after an orchestrator had already registered the wrong session.

options.option: Mint a session-scoped trigger phrase (`Start session N of `<slug>`.`)
options.consequence: An extension session would be defining a new orchestrator contract that lives in `docs/ai-led-session-workflow.md` and is honoured only by an LLM's goodwill â€” no gate enforces it. It also invites out-of-order starts, which the sequential lifecycle and the close gates assume cannot happen. Rejected as scope expansion, not deferred.

question: Step 4 wants the artifact menu entry to discover files by convention (`s<N>-*`) and to show an honest empty state. Should the entry be HIDDEN on sessions that have produced nothing â€” which would need a directory listing per session row on the tree scan â€” or always shown and answered at click time?
decision: Always show the entry; answer at click time. Hiding it would require reading every set directory during the tree scan to know whether `s<N>-*` exists, which is exactly the per-scan disk read Set 115's decision 4 and Set 110 S1's measured startup budget forbid. The read happens on the CLICK â€” the same seam Session 2 established for the spec read â€” and an empty result is reported as a plain informational message naming the session, the set and the `s<N>-*` convention, so the operator learns the rule from the empty state rather than from the docs. Discovery is `^s<N>-` on the top-level entries of the set directory, case-insensitively, files only, sorted by name: `s3-` cannot collide with `s30-` (the delimiter follows the digits), the prefix is the convention every existing artifact already obeys (`s1-issues.json`, `s2-verification-round-2.md`), and it mirrors the existing `ISSUES_FILE_RE` reader in `utils/fileSystem.ts` rather than inventing a second naming authority. One match opens directly; several open a QuickPick â€” the same shape `openPrerequisiteSpec` already uses.

options.option: Always show; discover and answer at click time (chosen)
options.consequence: No new I/O on any hot path, one code path for every session, and 'nothing yet' is a sentence the operator can act on. The cost is a menu entry that can lead to a message instead of a file.

options.option: Hide the entry when the session has no artifacts
options.consequence: A readdir per session row on every scan and every watcher tick â€” the measured constraint the set spent Session 1 protecting. It also makes 'no artifacts' indistinguishable from 'feature missing', which is a worse answer than the message.

options.option: Enumerate a hardcoded list of known artifact names
options.consequence: Explicitly refused by step 4. The set's own directory carries fourteen distinct `s1-*`/`s2-*` shapes today and gains new ones per set; a list would silently drop whatever a future session invents.

question: The close-out obligation projection is written mid-session, not at close. Where does it live, and is it version-controlled like session-progress.json? A tracked file in the session-set dir would be written after a verification round is stamped, which is the exact shape that sent Sets 111 S2, 112 S3 and 114 S1 into fresh metered rounds.
decision: Write it to <session-set-dir>/.dabbler/close-obligations.json, which is already gitignored repo-wide (the Set 029 entry 'docs/session-sets/*/.dabbler/'), and have the writer drop a self-protecting .gitignore inside the directory it creates so a consumer repo that never patched its root .gitignore is covered too - the same belt-and-suspenders Set 029 shipped for the marker files. Consequences, all of them structural rather than policy: the file cannot stale a verification stamp (git diff never sees an ignored path), it cannot fail working_tree_clean, it never lands in a reviewer's context or a consumer's diff, and close_session does not have to grow a 2-6 second write on the close path to keep it current. Absent is already a designed state (120 S3's vocabulary), so a fresh clone renders 'absent' honestly rather than rendering nothing.

options.option: Track it beside session-progress.json in the set dir.
options.consequence: Matches the 120 S3 precedent exactly, but every mid-session --write after a stamped round stales that round and buys a metered backstop round at close - the measured failure the CLOSE_MANDATED_WRITES mechanism was built for. Exempting it would mean either extending that mechanism to a write the close does not mandate (a lie in the declaration) or adding one more filename to WORK_DIFF_SET_BOOKKEEPING, which is the instance-not-class patch L-069-1 exists to stop.

options.option: Track it, and make close_session regenerate it so the CLOSE_MANDATED_WRITES declaration is honest.
options.consequence: Honest declaration, but it puts a 2-6 second git-backed computation on the close path to record a list that is by definition satisfied at that moment. Cost with no reader.

options.option: CHOSEN - an ignored cache under the set's .dabbler/ dir.
options.consequence: No stamp interaction, no close cost, no diff churn, and portable to consumer repos by construction. The cost is that the projection is per-machine: CI and a fresh clone see 'absent' until someone runs the preflight, which is the honest answer for a live operator aid and is exactly what the absent state is for.

rationale: Decided rather than escalated: placement and layout are orchestrator calls under the rubric. It resolves on prefer-reversible - an ignored cache can be promoted to a tracked artifact later with one path change, whereas a tracked artifact that has already staled rounds cannot un-spend them.

question: Two of the fourteen obligations (working_tree_clean, pushed_to_remote) are computed from git, not from files. No content digest can detect that they changed - committing does not alter any file the projection digests - so a projection can be provably fresh against its inputs and still be wrong about those two rows. What does the renderer show?
decision: Split the freshness question in two and say so in the file. 'inputs' carries the content digests any reader can recompute; 'volatileInputs' carries a git fingerprint (HEAD sha plus a digest of git status --porcelain) that only a reader able to run git can check. Every obligation derived from git carries volatile: true. The CLI's --check verifies both and reports stale when either moved; the tree, which deliberately never shells out, verifies the content digests and renders volatile rows with an explicit 'as of <time>' qualifier instead of as current truth. The git-backed check names are derived from the gate_checks source rather than hand-listed, and a test asserts the derivation against the constant, so a third git-backed predicate cannot quietly render as certain.

options.option: Digest only the files and let the two git rows ride the same freshness verdict.
options.consequence: Simplest file, and it produces the one failure the spec names as worse than no list at all: a projection badged fresh that says 'commit your work' after you committed, or worse, says nothing remains when a push does.

options.option: Drop the two git-backed obligations from the projection entirely.
options.consequence: Removes the state rather than adding one, which is the house preference - but the rendered list would then omit two real blocking obligations and could show an all-clear while a commit and a push stand between here and close. That is the silent lag the spec forbids.

options.option: Let the tree run git itself so it can check the fingerprint.
options.consequence: Exact, and it puts a process spawn on a tree that refreshes on every watcher tick - the same defect as calling the 6.6-second preflight from the renderer, only cheaper per call.

options.option: CHOSEN - two input classes, per-row volatility, and an 'as of' qualifier for the rows a given reader cannot recheck.
options.consequence: Each reader makes exactly the claim it can support. The cost is one more concept in the file's shape, paid to keep a renderer from asserting something it cannot know.

rationale: goal-over-letter: the letter of '120 S3's digest-based staleness' is one digest map, but its goal is that a cache can never be mistaken for a source. A single digest map would satisfy the letter and defeat the goal for two of fourteen rows.

question: Fourteen obligation rows under a session node that already expands to its steps. Flat beside the steps, or grouped under one child row?
decision: One 'Close-out' group row under the session, carrying the summary in its description (unmet blocking / advisory counts, or the projection's state when it is not fresh) and expanding to the obligation rows. The session node the operator watches gains one row, not fourteen; the detail is one click away; and the staleness verdict has a natural home on the parent rather than being repeated on every child.

options.option: Append the obligation rows beside the step rows.
options.consequence: No new node kind, but it triples the height of the row the operator watches during work, mixes two vocabularies (steps and gates) at one level with no visual separator, and leaves nowhere to put one staleness verdict.

options.option: CHOSEN - a single collapsible Close-out group row under the session.
options.consequence: One row added to the watched surface, an honest summary in its description, and the obligations behind a twisty. Costs a sixth node kind in the tree model and its descriptor - the same shape the fifth level already took.

options.option: Show only the UNMET obligations.
options.consequence: Shortest list, but 'what remains' with no denominator cannot be distinguished from 'the projection failed to compute anything', and a met row that flips back to unmet would appear from nowhere.

rationale: simpler-code decides it: the group row reuses the existing childrenOf / descriptorFor dispatch and keeps the step level's contract untouched, where the flat option would have to teach stepNodes about a second row species.

question: Spec step 4 names two sites for the marker removal (HERE_MARKER and its render). But the TypeScript derivation is wider - markHere, the isHere field, TERMINAL_STATUSES, a tooltip line, the parity corpus's expectedRows, two Python guards that exist only to protect the corpus's isHere, the Layer 2 tests and a Layer 3 spec. Remove the two named sites, or the whole derivation?
decision: Remove the whole derivation, in both languages, in one pass. sessionStepModel.ts loses markHere, TERMINAL_STATUSES and the isHere field; workExplorerTreeModel.ts loses HERE_MARKER, the tooltip line and the description render; the shared corpus loses isHere from every expectedRows entry; test_step_row_parity.py loses the two guards Set 120 S3 added to hold that field alive until this pass, and compares the full row again; the Layer 2 and Layer 3 assertions move onto what replaced it - the in-progress status reaching the icon. What the operator sees instead of the marker is the in-progress glyph on the step whose ledger status IS in-progress, which is a recorded fact rather than an inferred one.

options.option: Delete only the two sites the spec names.
options.consequence: Literal compliance, and it leaves markHere computing a field nothing renders - dead inference on the row model, still pinned by a corpus and by two Python guards that would now be protecting nothing. That is the same point-fix-reads-complete failure that produced this session (L-069-1).

options.option: CHOSEN - delete the derivation wholesale in both languages plus the corpus and every test that pins it.
options.consequence: The two implementations agree again with nothing left to prove agreement about, and the corpus's declared divergence disappears rather than being maintained. It touches the shared fixture and the tree model, so L-064-12's full Layer 3 obligation applies - which this session's step 5 already carries.

options.option: Keep isHere but drive the in-progress ICON from it instead of the status.
options.consequence: Reads like a faithful rendering of 'drop the marker, show the in-progress icon instead', and it would re-create the defect the ruling cites: the icon would follow an inference (first unfinished row) rather than the ledger, so it would point confidently at step 1 on bad data exactly as the marker did, and the two languages would disagree about which row is current with the parity corpus unable to see it.

rationale: goal-over-letter. The spec's letter names two lines; its stated goal is L-069-1 - fix every sibling site - and it says so in the same step. Set 120 S3's CHANGELOG explicitly deferred the wider removal to 'the carve', and the guards it left behind are addressed to whoever does this pass.

question: At the set's UAT walk the operator ruled 'Open Session Artifacts' out of the session row's context menu ('we no longer need Open Session Artifacts'). The ruling names the MENU. The command behind it is hidden from the Command Palette by design (`when: false` in package.json), so the menu was its only door. Remove the menu contribution alone, or the whole command with its discovery helpers and tests?
decision: Remove it wholesale. The `package.json` command declaration, the palette entry, the view/item menu contribution, the `SESSION_ACTIONS` entry, the `openSessionArtifacts` command registration and implementation, and the `isSessionArtifact` / `listSessionArtifacts` discovery helpers all go, along with the Layer 2 suite that drove the helpers and the two Layer 3 scenarios that drove the click. What REPLACES that coverage is an absence assertion at both layers: no session row emits the token, and the live context menu does not offer the label. The `clickRowMenuItem` Playwright helper written earlier this session to fix the CI race on those two scenarios goes too — it has no callers left.

options.option: Remove only the two `package.json` menu lines, exactly as the ruling is worded.
options.consequence: Minimal diff, and it leaves a registered command that nothing can invoke — hidden from the palette, absent from every menu — plus its implementation, its helpers and three test suites proving behaviour no operator can reach. Dead surface that reads as live, which is what the house rule about preferring removal exists to stop.

options.option: CHOSEN — remove the command, its helpers and the tests that only existed for it; keep absence assertions.
options.consequence: The menu offers exactly what the operator asked for and nothing is left behind. It also retires the two Layer 3 scenarios that were failing in CI on both platforms, so that failure is resolved by the surface going away rather than by the race fix — which is worth stating plainly rather than letting it read as a fix. Restoring the entry later means restoring code from git history, which is the cost of this option.

options.option: Keep the command and expose it in the Command Palette instead of the row menu.
options.consequence: Preserves the capability, but a palette command cannot know WHICH session the operator means — the whole reason it was `when: false` — so it would need a session picker that nobody asked for. Scope creep on the surface the set explicitly said is where scope creep lands.

rationale: The WHAT is the operator's (recorded in s4-uat-walk.md); the HOW FAR is a scoping call, which the rubric assigns to the orchestrator. It resolves on simpler-code: the alternative leaves a command, an implementation, two exported helpers and three test suites alive for a door that no longer exists.
